rv.q: In performance and direction, and in the small ways in which Caswell and Wills have plotted out this isolated love story, there’s a level of great richness and detail.
But Caswell’s underdeveloped script rather quickly loses interest in Arizonan particularities, and moves instead toward a generalized sense of grief.
More wizardry comes from Barbara Samuels’s lighting, which gorgeously slashes across the stage to illuminate Bruin in his white briefs, as if frozen in moonlight.
It’s a message that will resonate with anyone lucky enough to have enjoyed a healthy and rewarding long-term relationship, and should inspire everyone else.
And in Stephen Spinella's timing, precision, vocal prowess, and unbridled outpouring of honest but never excessive emotion, we have a master class: Folks, this is how it's done.
Caswell is dealing with unexplored territory in this lovely play, his plot and characterizations could use a bit more filling out.
The three actors feel out of sync, though.

John J. Caswell, Jr.’s throuple dramedy has its charms, but by treating one of its central leads as a puzzle to be solved, Jerome never reaches the spectacular emotional heights its script aims for in contending with queer history and grief.
There's plenty of interesting material here, but it needs focusing and more probing treatment; the characters' pasts are often more compelling than their present.
Caswell’s unfocused and not always credible play attempts with too little success to incorporate all those plots and more.
Jerome is a rewarding theatrical journey—one that balances intimacy with ambition, humor with heart, and romance with hard-earned wisdom.
A thoughtful and affecting drama about the dead who never entirely leave us.
The portrait of older gay men striving to hold on to life is empathetic.
The two plays also share some unfortunately flat, at times redundant dialogue, and, under Wills’s direction, there are long pauses and indulgent pacing that do little to help the action along.

Only in the last scene of the play, where Jerome provides the slightest glimmer of hope, does the play give us a glimpse of what it could have been: a gay positive, age-appropriate love story for audiences to embrace.
Ultimately, Jerome offers flashes of brilliance, but Caswell's play lacks the narrative cohesion and polish needed to bind its provocative ideas fully.
Too often, Jerome plays like the overlong first draft of a promising dramedy that hasn’t yet found its voice.

cn.t: Critics are mixed on this Arizona-set drama about an aging gay couple and a younger man navigating love and illness in the AIDS era, praising the performances (especially Spinella) but finding the direction unclear and the three-way relationship premise familiar.

vr.q: one of my favorite shows of the year so far

John J. Caswell Jr. has written really great dramatic scenes with multi-dimensional characters. This is a great play for actors, a great play for a director, and honestly, a great play for audiences. So, go check out Jerome.
I was fascinated by the dynamic this play presented, and while it had its clunky moments, it offered just as many funny or tender ones, too.
